title: Manulife's Third-Quarter Core Earnings Rise 4% to C$2.1 Billion and Core EPS Hits a Record C$1.24, While Reported Net Income Falls to C$1.4 Billion on Market Losses
summary: Manulife reported third-quarter 2026 core earnings of C$2,125 million, up 4% at constant exchange rates, with core EPS of C$1.24 and core ROE of 17.8%, while net income attributed to shareholders fell to C$1,424 million after a C$388 million post-tax market experience loss, and the contractual service margin grew to C$27.3 billion.
description:
Manulife Financial Corporation has published its results for the third quarter of 2026, the three months ended September 30. The press release is dated November 4, 2026, with an earnings call on November 5, and it was furnished to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Form 6-K. Manulife reports in Canadian dollars, with some segments shown in U.S. dollars as noted. Percentages and differences that are not in the release are calculated here and labelled. Manulife's own percentage changes for core measures are stated at constant exchange rates, so they can differ slightly from a simple comparison of the dollar figures.

Core earnings and reported earnings

The headline is a divergence. Core earnings, Manulife's preferred measure of underlying performance, were C$2,125 million, up 4% at constant exchange rates from C$2,035 million a year earlier. Core earnings per share (core EPS) were C$1.24 against C$1.16, up 6% by the release's measure. Core return on equity was 17.8% against 18.1%. In the release, chief executive Phil Witherington described the quarter as strong and said it achieved record core EPS and a 17.8% core return on equity.

Reported results moved the other way. Net income attributed to shareholders was C$1,424 million, against C$1,799 million in the third quarter of 2025. The release describes that as down 22%, while a direct comparison of the two dollar amounts gives about 21%, calculated here; the difference is probably the currency basis. Earnings per share were C$0.82 against C$1.02, and return on equity (the reported measure) was 11.8% against 16.0%.

Why the two measures diverged

Core earnings exclude items that Manulife regards as outside underlying performance, and the release lists the main ones. Market experience produced a net loss of C$388 million after tax, against a loss of only C$2 million a year earlier. The release attributes it to lower returns on alternative long-duration assets such as private equity, real estate and farmland, lower public equity returns, and derivative and hedge accounting losses. The annual review of actuarial assumptions had a net favourable effect on the balance sheet, with a C$128 million pre-tax decrease in fulfilment cash flows, but the updates that flow directly through income were a C$175 million post-tax charge. There was also a net charge in Vietnam, from a partial impairment of a bancassurance asset partly offset by a gain on the sale of a Vietnamese insurance subsidiary. Other items excluded from core earnings included a C$120 million charge for reinsurance, tax-related and other items, and C$18 million of amortisation of acquisition-related intangibles.

The release says core earnings growth was driven by Asia and the U.S., higher revenue in global wealth and asset management (Global WAM), and net positive actuarial updates in the quarter. These were partly offset by higher expected credit loss provisions and the transition to Hong Kong's eMPF platform for mandatory pension fund administration.

Segments

Asia produced core earnings of US$635 million against US$550 million, up 17% by the release's measure, while Asia net income attributed to shareholders was US$510 million against US$649 million. Canada's core earnings were C$440 million against C$428 million, up 3%, with net income of C$205 million against C$449 million. The U.S. segment earned US$254 million against US$241 million, up 5%, and its net income was US$137 million against a loss of US$54 million a year earlier. Global WAM's core earnings were C$503 million against C$525 million, down 5%, with net income of C$463 million against C$523 million. Corporate and Other core earnings were a loss of C$64 million against a loss of C$9 million.

Because the segments are shown in different currencies, this article does not add them together. The pattern is clear, though: Asia and the U.S. grew, Canada edged up and Global WAM slipped.

New business

New business measures were flat. APE sales, which standardise premiums across product types, were C$2,626 million, essentially unchanged from C$2,576 million. New business CSM, the amount of future profit added by new sales, was C$957 million, down 2% from C$966 million, and new business value was C$907 million against C$906 million. Global WAM net outflows were C$3.6 billion, compared with C$6.2 billion in the third quarter of 2025, so outflows narrowed.

The contractual service margin is the stock of unearned profit that a life insurer expects to recognise as it provides cover. Manulife's CSM net of non-controlling interests was C$27,318 million at September 30, 2026, up from C$24,969 million at December 31, 2025, an increase of about 9% calculated here. Total CSM was C$29,070 million, and post-tax CSM net of non-controlling interests was C$22,701 million.

Capital and shareholders

The LICAT ratio, the Canadian regulatory measure of life insurers' capital strength, was 136%. The financial leverage ratio was 23.0% against 22.7%. Book value per common share was C$28.06 against C$26.07, and adjusted book value per share was C$41.78 against C$38.22. Manulife returned C$1.3 billion to shareholders in the quarter. The release does not break out common dividends or share buybacks in the portions used here, and it lists preferred share dividends and other equity distributions of C$59 million for the quarter and C$220 million year to date. Chief financial officer Colin Simpson said the company remained disciplined in capital deployment.

What the release does not tell us

The release gives no guidance for future quarters, and this article does not forecast. It also does not explain how much of the market experience loss is likely to reverse. The release states the LICAT ratio but not the regulatory minimum it is measured against, so this article makes no judgement on capital adequacy. For investors, the quarter shows an insurer whose underlying earnings and CSM grew while reported profit was hit by investment valuations. The figures are the company's own, and readers should read the full release and consult a licensed adviser before making financial decisions.
source_name: Manulife Financial Corporation (third-quarter 2026 press release, Form 6-K filed with the SEC, November 4, 2026)
image_alt: Financial documents and calculator representing a life insurer's quarterly results (illustrative)
key_points: Core earnings were C$2,125 million, up 4% at constant exchange rates from C$2,035 million, and core EPS was C$1.24 against C$1.16, with core return on equity of 17.8% against 18.1%.

Net income attributed to shareholders was C$1,424 million against C$1,799 million, and EPS was C$0.82 against C$1.02, because market experience cost C$388 million after tax and an annual actuarial review charged C$175 million through income.
Asia core earnings rose 17% to US$635 million, Canada rose 3% to C$440 million and the U.S. rose 5% to US$254 million, while Global WAM fell 5% to C$503 million.

New business contractual service margin (CSM) was C$957 million, down 2%, annualised premium equivalent (APE) sales were flat at C$2,626 million, and the CSM balance net of non-controlling interests reached C$27,318 million from C$24,969 million at year-end 2025.
The LICAT ratio was 136%, book value per share was C$28.06, and Manulife returned C$1.3 billion to shareholders, though the release does not split that between dividends and buybacks.
why_it_matters: Manulife is one of North America's largest life insurers and a major player in Asia, so its results show how Asian demand and wealth-management markets are feeding a global insurer's profit. The gap between record core earnings per share and lower reported net income is a clear example of why life insurers steer investors to their own core measures.

title: Sun Life's Third-Quarter Underlying Net Income Rises 9% to C$1.15 Billion, but Reported Net Income Falls 29% to C$785 Million and Wealth Outflows Reach C$32.7 Billion
summary: Sun Life reported third-quarter 2026 underlying net income of C$1,146 million (C$2.05 per share, up 10%) and underlying ROE of 19.0%, while reported net income fell 29% to C$785 million on interest-rate effects and acquisition and restructuring charges; asset management and wealth saw net outflows of C$32.7 billion and the dividend rose to C$1.00.
description:
Sun Life Financial Inc. has reported results for the third quarter of 2026, the three months ended September 30. The release is dated November 4, 2026 and was furnished to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Form 6-K. Amounts are in Canadian dollars unless noted. Sun Life reports two profit measures, underlying net income, which excludes certain market-related and one-off items, and reported net income, which includes them, and this article covers both. Differences that are not in the release are calculated here and labelled.

Underlying earnings

Underlying net income was C$1,146 million, up 9% from C$1,047 million a year earlier. Underlying earnings per share on a diluted basis were C$2.05, up 10% from C$1.86, and underlying return on equity was 19.0% against 18.3%. All five lines that make up the total can be checked: asset management contributed C$416 million, Canada C$422 million, the U.S. C$197 million and Asia C$226 million, while the Corporate segment lost C$115 million. Those figures sum to C$1,146 million, calculated here, and the prior-year figures of C$387 million, C$397 million, C$147 million, C$211 million and a C$95 million loss sum to C$1,047 million.

By segment, Sun Life Asset Management grew 7% (6% in U.S. dollars, to US$297 million), Canada grew 6%, the U.S. grew 34% (32% in U.S. dollars, to US$141 million) and Asia grew 7%. The Corporate loss widened by C$20 million.

Reported earnings

Reported net income was C$785 million, down 29% from C$1,106 million, and reported earnings per share were C$1.40 against C$1.97. Reported return on equity was 13.0% against 19.3%. Underlying net income exceeded reported net income by C$361 million this quarter, calculated here, whereas a year earlier reported net income was C$59 million higher than underlying.

The release attributes the gap to unfavourable interest rate impacts of C$143 million after tax, acquisition and restructuring charges of C$126 million after tax, including a C$53 million restructuring charge and C$42 million of costs relating to the acquisition of Bell Partners, and unfavourable impacts from assumption changes and management actions, which Sun Life labels ACMA. The prior-year quarter had included a C$176 million gain from increased ownership in Bowtie, which helps explain why reported earnings were higher then.

Earlier in the year, the first quarter included a C$165 million charge for acquiring the remaining interests in a subsidiary named GreenOak and a C$145 million charge for a legal settlement in Canada. Those year-to-date items are separate from the third-quarter figures but show that reported results have been weighed down by a series of charges in 2026.

Sales and flows

In insurance, sales were solid. Group insurance sales rose 24% to C$619 million from C$498 million, and individual insurance sales rose 6% to C$1,042 million from C$987 million. New business contractual service margin (CSM), the profit expected from new sales, was C$385 million against C$446 million, and C$1,214 million for the year to date against C$1,287 million, both lower.

The weaker side is in asset management and wealth. Gross flows and wealth sales were C$54.4 billion, down 14% from C$63.1 billion. Net flows and wealth sales were outflows of C$32.7 billion, against inflows of C$3.1 billion in the third quarter of 2025. Assets under management still rose 3% to C$1,676 billion from C$1,623 billion, so market gains and other effects offset the outflows. The release does not break out the sources of the outflows in the portions used here, so this article does not attribute them to a particular client or product.

Capital and dividend

The LICAT ratio, the regulatory measure of capital strength for Canadian life insurers, was 142% for Sun Life Financial Inc. against 154% a year earlier, and 130% for its main operating insurer, Sun Life Assurance, against 138%. The declines are about 12 and 8 percentage points respectively, calculated here. The release does not explain the reasons in the portions used for this article. Sun Life raised the dividend from C$0.96 to C$1.00 per share, an increase of about 4% calculated here. The release does not mention share repurchases.

Strategic items

Two strategic items appear in the release. Sun Life announced a reinsurance and asset management partnership with Wilton Re, which is expected to launch in the first half of 2027 subject to approvals. It also referred to a C$5 billion commitment to Canadian infrastructure, which the release says depends on amendments to the Insurance Companies Act. Both are future plans, not completed transactions, and the release as used here does not give financial terms for them.

Management commentary

Chief executive Kevin Strain said in the release that Sun Life's diversified global strategy delivered robust continued momentum in insurance and wealth, led by Canada and Asia.

What to take away

For policyholders, the main facts are the capital ratios and the continued profitability of the insurance businesses. For investors, the quarter has a clear split: underlying earnings and insurance sales grew, but reported profit was lower and wealth flows turned sharply negative. How the outflows develop will matter for future earnings in the asset management arm. The release does not give forecasts, and this article does not predict. The figures are the company's own, and readers should read the full release and consult a licensed adviser before making financial decisions.

Reported net income fell 29% to C$785 million (C$1.40 per share) from C$1,106 million, as interest-rate effects (-C$143 million after tax) and acquisition and restructuring charges (-C$126 million) outweighed the underlying gains.
The U.S. segment grew most, with underlying net income up 34% to C$197 million, while Canada rose 6% to C$422 million, Asia rose 7% to C$226 million and asset management rose 7% to C$416 million.

The LICAT ratio for Sun Life Financial Inc. was 142% against 154%, and the quarterly dividend was raised from C$0.96 to C$1.00 per share.
why_it_matters: Sun Life is one of Canada's big three life insurers, with a large asset management arm and a growing business in Asia and the United States. The quarter shows healthy underlying earnings growth alongside a sharp reversal in wealth flows and a lower capital ratio, which are the measures to watch when reading the headline profit.

title: Aflac's Third-Quarter Net Earnings Drop to $303 Million After $1.1 Billion of Portfolio-Repositioning Losses, While Adjusted EPS Edges Down 2.4% to $2.43 and Japan's Margin Narrows
summary: Aflac reported third-quarter 2026 net earnings of $303 million ($0.61 per share) against $1.6 billion, after $1.1 billion of net investment losses from portfolio repositioning, while adjusted EPS fell 2.4% to $2.43; Aflac Japan's pretax margin fell to 44.4% from 52.2% and Aflac U.S. margin rose to 27.7%.
description:
Aflac Incorporated has reported results for the third quarter of 2026, the three months ended September 30. The earnings release, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission as Exhibit 99.1, is dated November 4, 2026, with a call the following morning. Aflac sells supplemental health and life insurance in Japan and the United States. Percentages and differences that are not in the release are calculated here and labelled. The release does not report the solvency margin ratio or a consolidated benefit ratio, so this article does not cover them.

Net earnings and adjusted earnings

Net earnings were $303 million, or $0.61 per diluted share, down from $1.6 billion, or $3.08 per share, in the third quarter of 2025. The release attributes the drop to net investment losses of $1.1 billion, or $2.15 per share, which came mainly from realized losses on portfolio repositioning. Total revenues were $3.3 billion, down 31.0%, because net investment losses are included in revenue. The release also records a $51 million tax valuation allowance, or $0.10 per share, on deferred tax assets tied to capital loss carryforwards. GAAP return on equity was 4.1%.

Aflac's preferred measure, adjusted earnings, tells a different story. Adjusted earnings were $1.2 billion, down 8.5%, and adjusted earnings per diluted share were $2.43, down 2.4%. Excluding the effect of currency, adjusted EPS was $2.46, down 1.2%. Adjusted earnings include $453 million of reserve remeasurement gains. Adjusted return on equity was 17.8% as reported and 23.7% excluding foreign currency remeasurement. The release does not explain the two ROE figures in more detail, so this article cites both as published.

For the nine months, net earnings were $2.1 billion, or $4.24 per diluted share, against $4.21 a year earlier, and adjusted earnings were $3.0 billion, or $5.92 per diluted share, flat year over year. Excluding currency, nine-month adjusted EPS was $6.02, up 1.7%. Nine-month revenues were $11.7 billion, down 4.6%.

What portfolio repositioning means

Realized losses on repositioning arise when an insurer sells investments for less than their carrying value, often to reinvest in assets the insurer considers better suited to its needs. These losses are real accounting charges, which is why net earnings fell so far, but they are excluded from adjusted earnings. The release does not say which assets were sold or what was bought, so this article does not describe the strategy. Net investment income was $1.0 billion, down 6.0%, and adjusted net investment income was $957 million, down 5.1%, so investment income did decline alongside the repositioning.

Aflac Japan

Aflac Japan's net earned premiums were ¥240 billion, or $1.5 billion, down 2.0% in yen and 9.3% in dollars. The gap between the two reflects exchange rates, since the yen weakened against the dollar over the period, which is an inference from the percentages and not a statement in the release. The release says premiums were affected by an external reinsurance deal in the first quarter and an internal reinsurance deal in the third quarter, and that Aflac Japan ceded roughly ¥500 billion of reserves on an FSA basis for cancer policies to Aflac Re Bermuda.

Pretax adjusted earnings were ¥152.3 billion, or $961 million, down 15.2% in yen and 21.0% in dollars. The pretax adjusted margin was 44.4% against 52.2%, and the benefit ratio, which is benefits paid and reserved as a share of premiums, rose to 49.2% from 39.3%. New sales were ¥18.8 billion, or $118 million, down 4.0%, and persistency, the share of policies kept in force, was 92.9%, down 40 basis points. The release as used here does not give a reason for the higher benefit ratio, and it would be speculation to name one.

Aflac U.S.

The U.S. business did better. Net earned premiums were $1.54 billion, up 3.3%, and pretax adjusted earnings were $493 million, up 31.5%. The pretax adjusted margin was 27.7% against 21.7%, and the benefit ratio improved to 40.7% from 45.6%. New sales were $403 million, up 3.5%, and persistency was 79.7%, up 70 basis points. Corporate and other pretax adjusted earnings were $72 million against $69 million.

Comparing the segments in dollars, calculated here, Aflac Japan's $961 million of pretax adjusted earnings was about twice Aflac U.S.'s $493 million, but Japan's contribution fell while the U.S. grew.

Balance sheet and capital return

Shareholders' equity was $29.3 billion, or $59.08 per share, and adjusted book value was $26.9 billion, or $54.21 per share. Aflac returned $1.1 billion to shareholders in the quarter, made up of $804 million of share repurchases and $305 million of dividends, which together equal $1,109 million, calculated here. The board declared a quarterly dividend of $0.61 per share, payable December 1, 2026 to holders of record on November 18, 2026, and the release says this marks 44 consecutive years of dividend increases.

Management view

Chief executive Daniel Amos said in the release that Aflac delivered solid adjusted earnings for the quarter and for the first nine months.

Reading the quarter

Three things stand out. First, most of the shortfall in net earnings comes from realized losses on repositioning the portfolio, which adjusted earnings exclude. Second, Aflac Japan's margin is lower, and the cause is not explained in the release. Third, Aflac U.S. is improving in both margin and benefit ratio. The release gives no outlook, and this article does not forecast. Policyholders should look at the company's financial strength ratings and claims-paying record, and investors should read the full release. This article is general information and not investment advice.

key_points: Net earnings were $303 million ($0.61 per diluted share) against $1.6 billion ($3.08), because net investment losses of $1.1 billion ($2.15 per share) came mainly from realized losses on portfolio repositioning.
Adjusted earnings were $1.2 billion, down 8.5%, and adjusted EPS was $2.43, down 2.4% (down 1.2% to $2.46 excluding currency), including $453 million of reserve remeasurement gains.
Aflac Japan's pretax adjusted earnings fell 15.2% in yen to ¥152.3 billion ($961 million), its pretax margin fell to 44.4% from 52.2% and its benefit ratio rose to 49.2% from 39.3%.
Aflac U.S. pretax adjusted earnings rose 31.5% to $493 million, with the margin up to 27.7% from 21.7% and the benefit ratio down to 40.7% from 45.6%.
Aflac returned $1.1 billion to shareholders ($804 million of buybacks and $305 million of dividends) and declared a $0.61 quarterly dividend, marking 44 consecutive years of dividend increases.
why_it_matters: Aflac is a major seller of supplemental insurance in both Japan and the United States, so its results show how two very different markets are performing. This quarter the large gap between net and adjusted earnings comes mainly from realized losses on portfolio repositioning, a reminder that net earnings and adjusted earnings can tell very different stories.

title: Prudential Financial's Third-Quarter Adjusted Operating Income Falls to $1.32 Billion as the Prudential of Japan Sales Suspension Cuts Japan Earnings 25%
summary: Prudential Financial reported third-quarter 2026 after-tax adjusted operating income of $1.321 billion ($3.77 per share) against $1.444 billion ($4.05), with net income of $1.388 billion ($3.96), as pre-tax Japan earnings fell to $559 million from $750 million, mainly because of the Prudential of Japan sales suspension.
description:
Prudential Financial, Inc. has reported results for the third quarter of 2026, the three months ended September 30. The earnings release, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission as Exhibit 99.1, is dated November 3, 2026, with a call the next day. The company reports net income, which follows U.S. accounting rules, and adjusted operating income, which excludes certain market and one-off items. Percentages and differences that are not in the release are calculated here and labelled. Note that the company has recast its segments in this report, so comparisons use the recast prior-year figures.

The headline numbers

After-tax adjusted operating income was $1.321 billion, or $3.77 per share, against $1.444 billion, or $4.05, a year earlier. That is a decline of about 8.5% in total and about 6.9% per share, calculated here, with the smaller per-share decline implying a lower share count. Net income attributable to Prudential Financial was $1.388 billion, or $3.96 per share, against $1.431 billion, or $4.01. Pre-tax adjusted operating income was $1,646 million against $1,829 million.

Segment results

Pre-tax adjusted operating income by segment was as follows, with prior-year figures in brackets. PGIM, the asset manager, earned $263 million ($244 million). U.S. Businesses earned $1,173 million ($1,188 million). Japan Businesses earned $559 million ($750 million). Corporate and Other lost $349 million (a loss of $353 million). Adding the four lines, $263 million plus $1,173 million plus $559 million less $349 million, gives $1,646 million, calculated here, matching the total. The prior-year lines sum to $1,829 million in the same way.

Within U.S. Businesses, Retirement earned $620 million ($637 million), Group Insurance $101 million ($90 million), Individual Life $199 million ($153 million) and U.S. Legacy Products $253 million ($308 million). Those four sum to $1,173 million, calculated here.

The Japan effect

The biggest change is in Japan. Pre-tax adjusted operating income there fell from $750 million to $559 million, a decline of about 25% calculated here. The release says the fall was mainly due to the Prudential of Japan sales suspension. Constant-dollar sales in Japan were $291 million, down 36%. Separate reporting says Japan's Financial Services Agency barred Prudential Life from new sales until January 31 after an employee fraud scandal; this article relies on the release for the earnings effect and does not describe the scandal itself.

The release also says the former International Businesses segment is now called Japan Businesses. Brazil and Mexico operations were moved to Divested and Run-off Businesses within Corporate and Other, and the 40% stake in a business called Habitat was moved to Retirement. These recasts mean the Japan Businesses segment now consists only of Japan.

PGIM

PGIM's assets under management were $1.465 trillion, essentially flat from a year earlier, and total net inflows in the quarter were $7.4 billion, including $9.0 billion from third-party clients. Total assets under management for the company were $1.616 trillion against $1.612 trillion. The release's figures show PGIM profit rising by about 8%, calculated here, from $244 million to $263 million.

Items between adjusted operating income and net income

Net income is higher than adjusted operating income in this quarter, by $67 million after tax, calculated here. The release lists notable items in net income, including $368 million of pre-tax net realized investment losses and related charges, of which $184 million were net credit-related losses, and $32 million of pre-tax losses from changes in market risk benefits. These were offset by $295 million of pre-tax earnings from divested and run-off businesses and $104 million of pre-tax gains from market experience updates. The release as used here does not give the after-tax effect of each item.

Capital and book value

Prudential returned $741 million to shareholders, comprising $250 million of share repurchases and $491 million of dividends, against $731 million a year earlier. The dividend was $1.40 per common share, which the release says is a yield of over 5% on adjusted book value. Parent company highly liquid assets were $4.0 billion against $3.9 billion.

Book value moved in opposite directions on the two measures. GAAP book value per share fell to $84.88 from $90.69, a decline of about 6% calculated here. Adjusted book value per share rose to $102.39 from $99.25, an increase of about 3%. The difference arises because adjusted book value excludes accumulated other comprehensive income and similar market-driven items, as the company defines it, so the release's two measures should be read together.

What the release does not say

The release as used here does not give an outlook, does not state the length of the Japanese suspension beyond the reference to it, and does not provide a forecast for when sales may recover. It also gives no after-tax split for each notable item. This article does not predict the recovery. Readers who want the exact definitions of adjusted operating income and the segment recasts should read the full release, and anyone making a financial decision should consult a licensed adviser. This article is general information and not investment advice.

key_points: After-tax adjusted operating income was $1.321 billion ($3.77 per share) against $1.444 billion ($4.05), and net income attributable to Prudential was $1.388 billion ($3.96) against $1.431 billion ($4.01).

Pre-tax adjusted operating income was $1,646 million against $1,829 million: PGIM $263 million, U.S. Businesses $1,173 million, Japan Businesses $559 million and Corporate and Other a loss of $349 million.

Japan Businesses earnings fell from $750 million to $559 million, which the release says was mainly due to the Prudential of Japan sales suspension, and constant-dollar sales were $291 million, down 36%.
PGIM assets under management were $1.465 trillion, essentially flat, with total net inflows of $7.4 billion including $9.0 billion of third-party inflows.

Capital returned was $741 million ($250 million of buybacks and $491 million of dividends), the dividend was $1.40 per share, and GAAP book value per share fell to $84.88 from $90.69 while adjusted book value rose to $102.39 from $99.25.
why_it_matters: Prudential Financial is one of the largest U.S. life insurers and a major global asset manager through PGIM, with a large business in Japan. The quarter shows what a regulator-imposed sales suspension does to earnings, and it separates that one-off Japan effect from the steadier U.S. and asset management businesses.

title: Lemonade's Third-Quarter In-Force Premium Jumps 34% to $1.55 Billion and Revenue Rises 73% to $336 Million, With the Net Loss at $43.7 Million and a Positive-EBITDA Quarter Promised for Q4
summary: Lemonade's third-quarter 2026 shareholder letter reports in-force premium up 34% to $1,550.8 million, 3.52 million customers, revenue up 73% to $336.1 million, a net loss of $43.7 million and adjusted EBITDA of negative $20.4 million, with guidance for its first positive adjusted EBITDA quarter in Q4 2026.
description:
Lemonade, Inc., the technology-led insurer, has published its third-quarter 2026 shareholder letter, covering the quarter ended September 30. The letter, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, does not state its own publication date but says Lemonade's earnings call will be held on November 5, 2026, and that an investor day will take place on November 17, 2026, in New York. Percentages and differences that are not in the letter are calculated here and labelled. The letter is a company document, and Lemonade defines adjusted EBITDA and several other measures itself, so readers should consult the definitions in the full letter.

Growth

In-force premium, the annualised premium on active policies at the end of the period, was $1,550.8 million, up 34% from $1,157.9 million a year earlier. Customers numbered 3,520,555, up 23% from 2,869,900. Premium per customer was $440, up 9% from $403, which is a sign that growth came from both more customers and more premium from each. Annual dollar retention, which in general terms measures how much premium stays on the books over a year, was 86%, up one percentage point.

Gross written premium was $450.7 million against $333.3 million, and gross earned premium was $364.1 million, up 33% from $274.7 million. Total revenue was $336.1 million, up 73% from $194.5 million. Revenue grew faster than earned premium, 73% against 33% as stated, and the letter extract used here does not explain the difference, so this article does not speculate on the cause.

Profitability

Gross profit was $118.1 million, up 48% from $79.9 million, but the gross profit margin fell to 35% from 41%. The gross loss ratio, which compares claims to gross earned premium, was 65% against 62%. Excluding catastrophes it was 63% against 56%, which means the ex-catastrophe loss ratio worsened by seven points. The net loss ratio was 64%, unchanged.

The net loss was $43.7 million, or $0.56 per share, against $37.5 million, or $0.51. Adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $20.4 million against a loss of $25.6 million, so the adjusted measure improved while the net loss widened. Adjusted free cash flow was $27.0 million against $18.1 million, and cash flow from operations was $7.3 million against $4.5 million. Cash and investments were about $1.2 billion, and about $350 million of regulatory surplus is required at the insurance subsidiaries. Employees numbered 1,321, down 1% from the second quarter.

Car insurance and Tesla

The car line is the main growth story. Car in-force premium was $265 million against $163 million, an increase of about 63% calculated here. The letter says car insurance is available in 14 states covering more than 50% of the U.S. population. Lemonade's Autonomous Car product has expanded to six states. Eligibility now includes Tesla vehicles with HW3 hardware, with a 30% lower rate on miles driven with Full Self-Driving (supervised) engaged, while HW4 vehicles get 50% off. Early conversion rates are more than twice those of the broader Car product, according to the letter.

These are company statements about pricing and conversion. The letter as used here does not give claims data for autonomous driving, and it is too early for this article to say whether the discount reflects lower losses.

Guidance

Lemonade's guidance for the fourth quarter of 2026 is in-force premium of $1,632 million to $1,639 million, gross earned premium of $379 million to $383 million, revenue of $342 million to $346 million, and adjusted EBITDA of $5 million to $9 million. For the full year, in-force premium guidance of $1,632 million to $1,639 million was reiterated, gross earned premium of $1,382 million to $1,386 million and revenue of $1,231 million to $1,235 million were both raised, and adjusted EBITDA is expected to be between negative $51 million and negative $47 million.

The company says it expects its first positive adjusted EBITDA quarter in Q4 2026 and its first full year of positive adjusted EBITDA in 2027. The chief executive's letter reiterates the expectation of positive adjusted EBITDA for the first time in Q4. Guidance is a forecast, not a result, and it can change.

A caution on the numbers

The quarter has a tension. Growth and revenue were strong, and the adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed, but the gross loss ratio worsened and the net loss widened. The Q4 target requires a swing from negative $20.4 million to between positive $5 million and $9 million in a single quarter, a change of roughly $25 million to $30 million calculated here. The letter does not break down how that improvement will happen in the portions used for this article. Insurance results can also swing with catastrophe losses, which the company excluded when giving its 63% loss ratio.

What it means

For customers, the points that matter are that Lemonade is growing quickly, that its insurance subsidiaries hold regulatory capital, and that car insurance now covers more than half the U.S. population. For investors, the guidance for Q4 is the key test. This article does not predict whether it will be met. Readers should read the full letter and the company's filings, and consult a licensed adviser before making financial decisions. This article is general information and not investment advice.

title: Corebridge Financial's Third-Quarter Operating EPS Rises 27% to $1.22 as the Share Count Falls 17%, With the Equitable Merger Reported to Be Making 'Significant Progress'
summary: Corebridge Financial reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted after-tax operating income of $545 million ($1.22 per share, up 27%), net income to common shareholders of $1,440 million, premiums and deposits down 29% to $8.8 billion, and common shares outstanding down to 440.3 million, while reporting significant progress toward its merger with Equitable.
description:
Corebridge Financial, Inc. has reported results for the third quarter of 2026, the quarter ended September 30. The press release, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, is dated November 2, 2026, with an earnings call on November 3. Corebridge is a provider of retirement solutions, including annuities, group retirement plans, life insurance and institutional products, and it has agreed to merge with Equitable. Percentages and differences that are not in the release are calculated here and labelled. The release gives its own definitions of adjusted measures, which readers should consult.

Net income and operating earnings

Net income available to common shareholders was $1,440 million, or $3.22 per diluted share, against $144 million, or $0.27, a year earlier. The release says the increase mainly reflects favorable net realized gains, including gains related to embedded derivatives on the Fortitude Re reinsurance arrangement and market risk benefits. These are accounting items that move with markets and are excluded from operating measures. Return on average equity on this net income basis was 70.3% against 4.5%, a figure that is a result of the unusually large gains and not a measure of underlying profitability.

Adjusted after-tax operating income, which Corebridge uses as its core earnings measure, was $545 million against $520 million, an increase of about 5% calculated here. Operating earnings per share were $1.22 against $0.96, up 27%. The gap between the 5% growth in dollars and the 27% growth per share is notable. It is consistent with the fall in common shares outstanding to 440.3 million from 532.1 million a year earlier, a decline of about 17% calculated here, though the release as used here does not itself link the two. Adjusted return on average equity was 12.1% against 10.3%, and adjusted book value per share was $41.37 against $38.03 at September 30, 2025.

Adjusted pre-tax operating income was $677 million against $654 million, up 4%, and the release's core sources of income measure was $1,545 million against $1,528 million, up 2%. Net investment income was $3,270 million against $3,320 million.

Segment results

Adjusted pre-tax operating income by segment, with prior-year figures in brackets: Individual Retirement $466 million ($451 million); Group Retirement $164 million ($185 million); Life Insurance $17 million ($25 million); Institutional Markets $198 million ($134 million); and Corporate and Other a loss of $168 million (a loss of $141 million). Adding them, $466 million plus $164 million plus $17 million plus $198 million less $168 million gives $677 million, matching the total, calculated here.

Institutional Markets grew 48%, which the release attributes to higher variable investment income. Group Retirement fell, Life Insurance fell and the Corporate loss widened.

Sales and deposits

Premiums and deposits, a measure of new money coming in, were $8,785 million against $12,290 million, down 29%. Excluding transactional activity, the decline was 19%. By segment, Individual Retirement fell 19% to $4,467 million, driven by lower fixed index annuity deposits. Group Retirement rose 1% to $1,780 million. Life Insurance was flat at $840 million. Institutional Markets fell 59% to $1,698 million, mainly from lower pension risk transfer premiums and deposits into guaranteed investment contracts.

Pension risk transfer, in which a company hands pension obligations to an insurer, tends to come in large, irregular deals, so quarter-to-quarter swings are common. That general point is context and is not from the release. The release does not say whether sales are expected to recover.

Capital, liquidity and returns

The release says the Life Fleet risk-based capital ratio is above target but gives no numeric figure. Holding company liquidity was $2.2 billion, including $750 million of pre-funded debt that matures in April 2027. The financial leverage ratio was 34.2%, including about 1.7 percentage points from the pre-funded debt. Corebridge returned $295 million to shareholders, $185 million of share repurchases and $110 million of dividends. The board declared a quarterly dividend of $0.25 per share, payable December 31, 2026 to holders of record on December 17, 2026.

The Equitable merger

The release reports significant progress toward completing the merger with Equitable, including advancing regulatory approvals, continuing preparations for the first day of the combined company and selecting members of the future board. Corebridge says it has identified more than $100 million of expense synergies. Completion remains subject to regulatory and other approvals. Separate reporting indicated that the companies' stockholders approved the all-stock merger on July 30 and that closing was expected by the end of 2026; this article relies on the release for the current status, which says only that approvals are advancing.

Management comment

Chief executive Marc Costantini said the third-quarter results highlight the strength of the company's diversified business model, resilient earnings profile and disciplined approach to capital allocation.

What to take from the quarter

Three observations follow from the numbers. Per-share growth is well ahead of dollar growth because the share count has fallen sharply. New money fell, with the largest declines in fixed index annuities and pension risk transfer. And the net income figure is very large mainly because of market-driven gains that should not be read as recurring profit. The release does not provide a forecast, and this article does not predict. Anyone making a financial decision should read the full release and consult a licensed adviser. This article is general information and not investment advice.

key_points: Adjusted after-tax operating income was $545 million against $520 million, and operating EPS was $1.22 against $0.96, up 27%, helped by common shares outstanding falling to 440.3 million from 532.1 million.

Net income available to common shareholders was $1,440 million ($3.22 per diluted share) against $144 million ($0.27), mainly because of favorable net realized gains, including from Fortitude Re embedded derivatives and market risk benefits.

Adjusted pre-tax operating income rose 4% to $677 million, with Individual Retirement at $466 million, Group Retirement at $164 million, Life Insurance at $17 million and Institutional Markets up 48% to $198 million.

Premiums and deposits fell 29% to $8,785 million (down 19% excluding transactional activity), as Individual Retirement deposits fell 19% on lower fixed index annuity sales and Institutional Markets deposits fell 59%.

Corebridge returned $295 million ($185 million of buybacks and $110 million of dividends), holds $2.2 billion of holding company liquidity, and reports significant progress toward the Equitable merger with more than $100 million of identified expense synergies.
why_it_matters: Corebridge is one of the largest U.S. sellers of retirement annuities and is in the middle of a planned all-stock merger with Equitable. Its results show how much of its per-share profit growth comes from buybacks and how sales are shifting, which matters for anyone holding its annuities or following the merger.
